blocks.text: Jenny thought the editor wanted another correction when he called her away from her typewriter. Instead, he held a framed certificate.
Her article about the Defenders had won a journalism prize.
“Good work, Jenny,” he said. “You got the story, and you got it right.”

blocks.alt: Jenny, in her ordinary reporter clothes, receives a framed journalism award from her editor as colleagues applaud in the Cleveland Defender newsroom.
blocks.text: He handed her the award. Someone started clapping, and the rest of the newsroom joined in. Jenny looked down at her name beneath the glass. For once, she could not think of a question.
Then the editor told her about the promotion. More responsibility. More stories of her own. He wanted her following the news, not waiting for assignments to reach her desk.
Jenny thanked him twice. Back at her typewriter, she set the certificate where she could see it and tried to stop smiling long enough to work.
Before the afternoon was over, there were already more notes beside her telephone.
She wanted this. She had worked for it. But every new assignment meant calls, interviews and hours getting the facts right. None of that could be finished by moving her legs faster.
That evening, she brought the award home and stood it beside her notebook. Her white mask lay nearby, ready for the next rooftop practice.
Jenny picked it up. What would she do when a deadline and someone needing help arrived at the same time? How would she find time for work, training, Seth—and a little life of her own?
It was nearly time for rooftop practice. She set the mask beside her notebook and began changing.
She would have to find a way. She just did not know what it was yet.
